title: Free voice dictation that replaced a paid app
what_it_does: A Windows tray app: press a hotkey from any app, talk, and your words land wherever the cursor is. Groq's Whisper transcribes (or a free model running on your own machine), an optional AI pass fixes punctuation and filler words, and it pastes the result. It transcribes in chunks while you speak, so a five-minute dictation is ready about a second after you stop. Open source.
why: He was paying $12 a month for Wispr Flow, a dictation app he uses every day. The tech under it costs almost nothing to call directly, so he built his own in about 2 hours. It runs for about $0.04 per hour of audio on Groq, or $0 fully offline, and he still uses it daily for emails, messages and long writing.
integrations: A global hotkey and your microphone, so it starts from any app (Python keyboard and audio libraries)
A speech-to-text model that's fast and cheap (Groq Whisper, or Parakeet and faster-whisper offline for $0)
An optional small AI model to clean up punctuation and filler words (Groq)
Your clipboard, to paste the text at the cursor

flow.eg: Groq Whisper or a local model

Ask me first: 1) Windows or Mac, 2) whether I'm OK sending audio to a cloud API or want it fully offline, 3) which hotkey I'd use. AI cleanup, custom vocabulary and a tray icon come after the basic loop works.

why: Great moments from calls were stuck inside hour-long recordings. Cutting them by hand meant scrubbing video and fighting Zoom's laggy burned-in captions.

A speech-to-text model with word timings, to cut on exact words (faster-whisper, free)

title: Alumni outreach CRM
what_it_does: A one-page CRM for personally reaching about 300 past students. Each person gets a card with a drafted message in their language, personalized with their name and what they built. One click opens WhatsApp with the text filled in, he records a voice note, and the card moves along the pipeline with today's date. A chat co-pilot answers "where did we leave off?" and flags anyone who hasn't replied in a week. A live counter shows how many he has sent today, a filter shows only people with a name on file, and cards without a name have a box for the name from their WhatsApp profile, plus a ready-to-copy contact label like "Maria (Nomad Cruise 17)". First day: 28 people contacted, 20 in one focused hour, against a target of 5 to 10.
why: He wanted to personally contact every alumnus in daily two-hour blocks, and keeping 300 conversations straight in his head and in WhatsApp wasn't going to work.
integrations: Spreadsheet access, to import the contact list (Google Sheets)
A place to host the page and save its data (Claude artifact, Cloudflare)
WhatsApp click-to-chat links, to open a chat with the message filled in (no API needed)
An AI chat, to draft personal messages and run the co-pilot (Claude)

title: Scheduled WhatsApp group messages
what_it_does: Queues WhatsApp messages to set groups at set times from his own number and sends them on time, with a confirmation ping after each one. Any of his AI sessions can add, change or cancel a message, or set a repeating one like "every other Saturday at 9am, rotate these texts", through one private web address with no laptop on. Each queue can only post to its own groups and follows quiet hours and each group's posting window. It runs the Silent Book Club reminders and the HvR community prompts.
why: Group reminders and community prompts went out by hand, and the first automated version needed his PC switched on to load each batch.
integrations: A WhatsApp account linked as a device on an always-on server, to send the messages (Baileys on a small VPS)
A private web address with a secret token, so AI sessions can add, change and cancel messages (a small Node server)
A list of allowed groups per queue, so nothing posts somewhere new without review (a JSON file in the repo)
Optional: a WhatsApp Cloud API number, for sent and failed pings (Meta)

title: One call into a week of episodes and shorts, overnight
what_it_does: After a recorded group call, it cuts the whole ladder while we sleep: full episodes, standalone segments, vertical shorts, a clip per tool we built, teasers and a few experiments. Each piece is defined by the spoken words it starts and ends on, so cuts land on exact words. It removes dead air, evens out quiet speakers, adds titles and captions, then a separate AI reads each piece cold and flags anything a new viewer wouldn't follow. Everything lands in Drive and a Notion media library as drafts for a morning review.
why: One two-hour live session holds a week of content, but editing it by hand takes days. The first run turned one call into 27 videos in about an hour and a half, and Alex only reviews, he doesn't edit.

A speech-to-text model with word timings (faster-whisper, free)
